promptText: What is the classic race-condition bug in a naive useEffect plus fetch data-fetching pattern?
options: If a dependency changes quickly (e.g. fast typing), two requests can be in flight, and if the older request resolves after the newer one, its stale response overwrites the fresher data
fetch() cannot be called inside useEffect at all without throwing a syntax error
useEffect always cancels in-flight requests automatically, causing data to never load
The browser blocks more than one fetch call per component by default
explanation: The network is not FIFO, so nothing guarantees the newest request resolves last; without cancellation or a stale-response guard, an older response can overwrite the current, correct data.

promptText: Why must you check err.name === 'AbortError' and return early after calling controller.abort() in cleanup?
options: Aborting a fetch rejects its promise with an AbortError, which is an expected outcome of cancellation, not a real failure — without this check, you'd incorrectly show an error UI on cancellation
Because AbortController does not actually cancel the network request, only the promise
Because without this check, the component would never re-render again
Because AbortError only occurs in server-side rendering, never in the browser
explanation: Abort deliberately rejects the fetch promise; treating that rejection as a genuine error would incorrectly flash an error state every time a request is superseded and cancelled.

promptText: Why is 'server state' considered fundamentally different from ordinary client state?
options: It's asynchronous, owned by a remote server, can go stale, and is often shared across users or tabs — requiring caching, deduplication, and revalidation that plain client state managers don't provide
Server state can only ever be read once and never updated again
Server state must always be stored using GraphQL, never REST
There is no real difference; both are just JavaScript values in memory
explanation: Client state is synchronous and fully owned by the app; server state is a cache of remote truth that can change without the app knowing, needing an entirely different set of tools.

promptText: Why is modeling fetch state as a discriminated union (status: idle | loading | success | error) preferred over three independent booleans (loading, error, data)?
options: Independent booleans allow impossible combinations, such as loading and error both true simultaneously; a single status field makes such invalid states unrepresentable and lets consumers narrow safely
Booleans are slower to compare than string literals in JavaScript
TypeScript cannot type boolean fields on an object at all
A discriminated union uses less memory than three booleans
explanation: With three loose fields, consumers must defensively check combinations that shouldn't exist; a tagged union forces exactly one valid state at a time and TypeScript narrows the rest automatically.

promptText: In TanStack Query, what determines whether two components share one cached entry and one in-flight request?
options: Using the identical (serializable) queryKey — matching keys means the same cache entry, deduplicated automatically
Being rendered inside the same parent component
Calling useQuery in the same file
Using the same variable name for the destructured result
explanation: The query key is the cache identity; components with the same key share the cache entry and dedupe concurrent in-flight requests regardless of where they live in the tree.

promptText: What is the precise distinction between staleTime and gcTime (formerly cacheTime) in TanStack Query?
options: staleTime controls how long data is considered fresh enough to skip a background refetch while in use; gcTime controls how long an inactive, unobserved query stays in memory before being deleted
They are aliases for the exact same setting, just renamed across major versions
staleTime only applies to mutations, while gcTime only applies to queries
gcTime determines how many retries a failed query gets before giving up
explanation: staleTime governs refetch behavior while the query is being used; gcTime governs eviction of unused cache entries once no component observes them anymore — two orthogonal concerns.

promptText: Why do teams commonly raise staleTime above its default of 0 for data that doesn't change every second?
options: With the default staleTime of 0, data is immediately stale, triggering refetches on nearly every mount or focus; a higher staleTime skips redundant background refetches for data that's still valid
Because a staleTime of 0 causes TanStack Query to never cache anything at all
Because staleTime of 0 disables mutations from working correctly
Raising staleTime is required before any query can use the enabled option
explanation: A staleTime of 0 means data is stale the instant it arrives, so it refetches on the next focus or mount; setting a sensible staleTime avoids unnecessary background traffic for slow-changing data.

promptText: When implementing an optimistic update, why must you call queryClient.cancelQueries inside onMutate before writing the optimistic value?
options: To stop a refetch that was already in flight from resolving after your optimistic write and overwriting it with stale pre-mutation data
Because mutations cannot run at all while any query is in flight anywhere in the app
To prevent the mutation itself from being cancelled by the user
It's purely a convention with no functional effect on the cache
explanation: Without cancelling first, a background refetch already in progress when the mutation starts can resolve after the optimistic write and clobber it with the old, pre-mutation data.

promptText: Why should a retry policy generally return false (don't retry) for a 404 or 401 response but retry a 503?
options: A 404/401 represents a request that will never succeed no matter how many times it's retried, whereas a 503 (service unavailable) is often a transient condition likely to succeed on retry
404 and 401 status codes are not valid HTTP codes and cannot be handled by retry logic
Retrying is always beneficial regardless of status code, so this distinction doesn't matter in practice
503 errors should never be retried because they always indicate a permanent outage
explanation: Retrying a request whose failure is deterministic (wrong resource, invalid auth) wastes time and delays showing the real problem; transient infrastructure errors are the right candidates for retry with backoff.

promptText: In a component under <Suspense>, calling useSuspenseQuery twice sequentially for independent data causes a request waterfall. Why, and how does useSuspenseQueries fix it?
options: The component function stops executing at the first hook that suspends, so any hook call textually after it hasn't run yet and its fetch hasn't started; useSuspenseQueries issues all the queries together before suspending once, so they start concurrently
Suspense itself throttles all network requests to one at a time regardless of which hook is used
useSuspenseQuery always waits for a hardcoded 1-second delay before firing
There is no actual waterfall; both queries always fire in parallel regardless of which hook you use
explanation: React re-attempts a suspended render later, meaning code after the first suspending hook simply hasn't executed yet; batching queries with useSuspenseQueries starts every fetch before any suspension occurs.

promptText: What's the key architectural difference between offset pagination (?page=2) and cursor pagination (?after=<id>) under concurrent writes?
options: Offset pagination drifts when rows are inserted or deleted, since items shift between pages, while cursor pagination anchors each page to a stable row key and stays correct regardless of concurrent mutation
Cursor pagination cannot be combined with infinite scroll under any circumstances
Offset pagination is always faster at the database level, regardless of table size
There is no functional difference; the two are interchangeable in every scenario
explanation: A row inserted or deleted while a user is on offset page 2 shifts subsequent items, causing duplicates or skipped rows; cursor pagination avoids this because each page is anchored to a real, stable key.

promptText: In TanStack Query, what is the main purpose of a 'query key factory' module such as todoKeys.list(filters) and todoKeys.detail(id)?
options: It centralizes the exact shape of every query key so call sites and invalidation calls can never drift apart due to a typo, and supports invalidating at a chosen level of granularity
It replaces the need for a queryFn entirely
It automatically generates TypeScript interfaces for API responses
It is required syntax for useQuery to function at all
explanation: Because keys are matched by structural equality and prefix, a typo in a hand-typed key silently creates a disconnected cache entry; a factory eliminates that risk and documents the key hierarchy.

promptText: How does request deduplication work when ten components mount useQuery with the identical query key in the same render pass?
options: They all register as observers of the same single cache entry; if a fetch is already in flight for that key, the existing promise is reused rather than firing ten separate network requests
Each component fires its own independent request, and TanStack Query discards nine of the ten responses afterward
Only the first-mounted component gets data; the other nine permanently show a loading state
Deduplication only works if all ten components are children of the same immediate parent
explanation: Each unique query key maps to one query object with one in-flight promise; every useQuery call becomes an observer of that same entry rather than triggering its own independent fetch.

promptText: When integrating real-time updates (WebSocket or SSE) with a query cache, why is it considered correct to write incoming messages directly into the query cache via setQueryData rather than maintaining a separate 'realtime state' store?
options: It keeps the query cache as the single source of truth regardless of whether data arrived via fetch or push, so every component reads it identically without needing to reconcile two parallel copies of the same data
setQueryData is the only function capable of accepting data from a WebSocket message handler
A separate realtime store is always faster because it avoids React's reconciliation entirely
WebSocket messages cannot be processed inside a useEffect, so they must go through the query cache
explanation: Routing pushed updates through the same cache ordinary fetches populate means every component behaves identically regardless of data origin, avoiding a parallel state store that could disagree with the cache.

promptText: In a shared auth/fetch layer, why is a 'single-flight' refresh promise necessary when ten requests all receive a 401 at the same time?
options: Without it, all ten would independently call the refresh endpoint concurrently, potentially rotating or invalidating the refresh token against itself and logging the user out; queuing them behind one shared refresh call avoids that
Because the browser only allows one HTTP request in flight at any given time
Because refresh tokens can only be used exactly once per page load regardless of concurrency
It has no real benefit; ten simultaneous refresh calls are functionally harmless
explanation: A shared in-flight refresh promise ensures concurrent 401s await the same refresh attempt and retry with the new token, rather than triggering a refresh stampede that can rotate the token against itself.
